findings.detail: Checked at the relaxed sensitivity set in Settings. No clipping, vibration, estimator rejection, motor imbalance, RC loss or low battery reached that level. The plots still show everything, and anything listed under this line is context rather than a problem.
PX4 also selects that for itself on a failsafe. Nothing else in this log says a failsafe fired, so if the pilot did not ask for it, the reason is in the messages below.

Checked at the normal sensitivity set in Settings. No clipping, vibration, estimator rejection, motor imbalance, RC loss or low battery reached that level. The plots still show everything, and anything listed under this line is context rather than a problem.
PX4 also selects that for itself on a failsafe. Nothing else in this log says a failsafe fired, so if the pilot did not ask for it, the reason is in the messages below.

plots.title: Ground track
plots.note: Local position, north up, equal axes. Origin is where the estimator started, not a survey point. GPS is projected through the estimator's own origin, so a gap between the two tracks is estimator error and not a difference of frames.

plots.title: Local position Z (height)
plots.note: Flipped out of NED so up is up. Zero is where the estimator started, not the ground.

plots.title: Velocity Z (climb)
plots.note: Flipped out of NED, so a climb reads as a climb.

plots.title: Estimated wind
plots.note: Estimated, not measured, but a climbing estimate explains a lot of otherwise puzzling tracking error.

plots.title: Manual control input
plots.note: The pilot's side of every control plot above. A rate that only misbehaves while a stick is moving is a different problem from one that misbehaves on its own.

plots.title: Roll angle
plots.note: The estimate should sit on the setpoint. A steady offset is trim or tuning; a sudden divergence is not.

plots.title: Roll angular rate
plots.note: Lag behind the setpoint means the gains are low; overshoot and ringing mean they are high.

plots.title: Pitch angle
plots.note: The estimate should sit on the setpoint. A steady offset is trim or tuning; a sudden divergence is not.

plots.title: Pitch angular rate
plots.note: Lag behind the setpoint means the gains are low; overshoot and ringing mean they are high.

plots.title: Yaw angle
plots.note: Yaw wraps at ±180°, so a jump between the two is the wrap, not the aircraft. Watch the gap between the pair instead.

plots.title: Yaw angular rate
plots.note: Lag behind the setpoint means the gains are low; overshoot and ringing mean they are high.

plots.title: Rate tracking error
plots.note: Setpoint minus measured, so zero is perfect. A trace that sits off zero means the aircraft could not deliver what was asked; one that buzzes about zero means the gains are chasing noise.

plots.title: Thrust demand
plots.note: Read the vibration and current plots against this: both are expected to rise with thrust.

plots.title: Motor outputs
plots.note: A motor sitting at its limit while the others do not is an imbalance. Check the airframe, not the tuning.

plots.title: ESC RPM
plots.note: Reported by the ESCs, not commanded. One motor consistently faster than its neighbours is carrying more of the airframe; one that drops out and returns is a motor or an ESC on its way out.

plots.title: EKF innovation test ratios
plots.note: 1.0 is the rejection threshold: above it the estimator is discarding that sensor. Brief spikes are normal, a sustained excursion is not.

plots.title: Altitude estimate
plots.note: The three sources should track each other. GPS stepping away is a fix problem; the barometer drifting away is weather or prop wash reaching the sensor. The fused estimate sitting away from its setpoint is neither. that is the controller.

plots.title: Horizontal velocity: GPS vs estimate
plots.note: A persistent gap between the two is the estimator distrusting GPS. Cross-read it against the innovation test ratios.

plots.title: Estimated gyro bias
plots.note: Bias should settle and stay put. One that keeps walking is a gyro worth replacing.

plots.title: Vibration metrics
plots.note: Read against the thrust plot: a level that climbs with throttle is a propeller or motor problem, not a tuning one. PX4 treats roughly 30 as the point to act on and 60 as the point the estimator suffers.

plots.title: Magnetic field strength
plots.note: A flat line is what you want. Movement that tracks throttle is interference from the power wiring, and it is what makes a compass calibration not stick.

plots.title: IMU temperature
plots.note: A sensor still warming up drifts. A cold first flight of the day is where that shows.

plots.title: Barometer
plots.note: Barometric altitude drifts with temperature and with air moving over the sensor. A reading that walks while the aircraft sits still is the sensor, not the aircraft.

plots.title: GPS uncertainty
plots.note: This is what the receiver claims, not what it achieved. A value that climbs while the satellite count holds is usually multipath. Read it with the noise plot below.

plots.title: GPS noise and jamming
plots.note: A jamming indicator that rises with throttle is almost always the aircraft's own power wiring or video transmitter, not somebody else's jammer.

plots.title: GPS fix type
plots.note: Below 3 there is no 3-D fix, and every position plot above is running on dead reckoning.

plots.title: Battery
plots.note: A voltage that dives under throttle and recovers is a tired pack, and it is the reading that decides whether the next flight is a good idea.

plots.title: RC link
plots.note: A signal-lost flag that goes high in flight is a failsafe waiting to happen.
